events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands of people in the United States. Communities mourn and help those affected.

events.title: Apple introduces the iPod
events.description: A pocket-sized digital music player becomes a new product for the computer maker.

events.title: Euro cash enters everyday use
events.description: Twelve countries introduce euro notes and coins.

events.title: Columbia is lost
events.description: The space shuttle breaks apart during its return to Earth, killing its seven crew members.

what_happened_next.text:
Occidental Petroleum led these choices, ending at about $3.49 per starting dollar. Apple reached roughly $1.48, while Amazon finished near 67 cents. The U.S. share basket ended lower, but bonds gained. The internet was exciting at the start, yet that label did not describe every business or guarantee that online shares would rise.

There were important company changes. Apple said more than two million iPods had sold by January 2004. Occidental bought Altura Energy, a major Texas oil producer, and later reported fourth-quarter earnings more than 80% above the year before. Amazon’s 2003 sales grew 34% and it reported a small annual profit, yet its share still ended lower. Stronger company results do not always mean stronger share returns over the same dates.

The five years included the September 11 attacks, euro notes and coins entering daily use, and the loss of the Columbia shuttle and its seven crew members. None of that future history was visible on the January 2000 starting page. If money were spread across choices, gains and losses would combine; the most talked-about industry was not the only possible place to invest.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Online shopping, technology wealth and executive rewards filled the news. An oil-drilling dispute showed that older industries still mattered too.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The seven investments followed different paths. Bonds gained while the broad US basket fell, and even the two technology-related companies had different results.
reflection.what_faded_away: A famous leader’s reward and an online-shopping stunt did not predict five-year returns. Public attention was not the same as investment value.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew the final ranking or the crises ahead. It would have been easy to overlook a less fashionable industry while reading exciting technology stories.

hot:2000-01:apple.text: Apple announced on January 6, 2004, that it had sold more than two million iPods since launch. The portable music player gave Apple a fast-growing business alongside Mac computers, reaching people who wanted a digital music device.

hot:2000-01:occidental.text: Occidental completed its purchase of Altura Energy in April 2000, adding a major Texas oil producer. In January 2001, it reported fourth-quarter earnings before special items up more than 80% from a year earlier, alongside higher sales and production.

hot:2000-01:amazon.text: Amazon’s 2003 sales grew 34% to $5.26 billion, and it earned $35 million after losing $149 million the year before. Lower prices and broader product choices attracted customers, while better cost control helped turn sales into profit. Still, Amazon’s share ended below its January 2000 starting value.
